transcript.text:
The missing number is 4, making the equivalent fraction 4/6.

Here is how to solve it:

Compare the denominators (bottom numbers): Look at how 3 becomes 6. Since 3 × 2 = 6, the denominator was multiplied by 2.

Multiply the numerator (top number) by the same amount: To keep the fraction equal, multiply the top number by 2 as well:

2 × 2 = 4

So, 2/3 = 4/6.
I get that the answer is four, but I don't get why you multiply both numbers by the same thing.

Multiplying both numbers by the same thing is just a math trick for multiplying by 1, which changes how a number looks without changing its actual value.

Here is why it works in two different ways:

1. The Pizza Slice Way (Visual)

Imagine a pizza cut into 3 large slices, and you have 2 of them (2/3).

Now, imagine you take a pizza cutter and slice every single piece right down the middle (multiplying the total pieces by 2):

Because you cut every slice in half, the whole pizza now has 6 slices instead of 3 (bottom number × 2).

Your 2 big slices also got cut in half, so you now hold 4 smaller slices (top number × 2).

You still have the exact same amount of pizza—you just cut it into smaller pieces.

2. The "Secret 1" Way (Math Rule)

In math, any number multiplied by 1 stays the exact same value (5 × 1 = 5).

Also, any fraction where the top and bottom numbers are the same equals 1 (for example, 2/2 = 1, because 2 divided by 2 is 1).

So when you multiply both the top and bottom of 2/3 by 2, you are actually doing this:

2/3 × 2/2 = 4/6

Because 2/2 is really just 1, you haven't changed the true size of 2/3 at all—you've just dressed it up in different numbers.

Would you like to test this out or see how it works in reverse?
OK. But I don't get why.

Think of it like a recipe or a photo: you are changing the scale, but not the recipe.

Imagine a pancake recipe that calls for 2 cups of flour for every 3 cups of milk (written as the fraction 2/3).

If you want to make a bigger batch for a lot of friends, you have to double everything equally.

You double the flour (2 × 2 = 4) and you double the milk (3 × 2 = 6), giving you 4/6.

Why does this matter?
If you accidentally doubled only the flour and forgot to double the milk, your pancakes would turn into thick, dry bricks. The recipe would be ruined because the relationship between the ingredients changed.

A fraction is just a relationship (a ratio) between two numbers:

The bottom number tells you how many total parts make up the whole.

The top number tells you how many parts you actually have.

If you multiply only the top number, you're claiming you suddenly have more pieces out of nowhere without changing the size of the whole. But if you multiply both by 2, you are scaling the whole thing up in perfect balance. The pieces get split, and your share gets split by the exact same amount, keeping the actual amount you have completely identical.
